answer.question: My mom just turned 65 and is signing up for Medicare. How much will her Part B premium be each month in 2026, and is there anything that could make it higher?
answer.answer:
The standard Part B premium in 2026 is $202.90 a month, and most people pay that amount. Two things can make it higher:

1. Income. Medicare uses the modified adjusted gross income reported on the IRS tax return from 2 years ago to set the premium, so a higher income can mean a higher amount (an extra amount called IRMAA).
2. A late enrollment penalty. If she doesn't sign up for Part B when she's first eligible, her monthly premium may go up 10% for each full 12 months she could have had Part B but didn't sign up, and she'd pay that penalty for as long as she has Part B. (She may not owe the penalty if she signs up during a Special Enrollment Period or enrolls in a Medicare Savings Program.)

Her Initial Enrollment Period is generally the 7-month period that begins 3 months before the month she turns 65 and ends 3 months after that month, so signing up in that window avoids the penalty. If she gets Social Security or Railroad Retirement Board benefits, the premium is deducted from her monthly benefit payment; otherwise she'll get a bill, typically quarterly.

answer.question: Dad has Original Medicare and no other insurance. He spent 5 days in the hospital and then went straight into a skilled nursing facility for 30 days. What will he owe for that in 2026?
answer.answer:
Based on the handbook's 2026 Part A amounts, here's how it works out.

Hospital (5 days as an inpatient): He pays the $1,736 Part A deductible for the benefit period, and then $0 each day for days 1–60.

Skilled nursing facility (SNF) (30 days): Because the hospital stay and the SNF stay are in the same benefit period, he doesn't pay the $1,736 deductible again — "you don't have to pay the Part A deductible for skilled nursing facility care if you already paid it for care you got in a hospital during the same benefit period." For SNF days 1–20 he pays $0 each day; for days 21–100 he pays $217 each day. So days 21–30 is 10 days × $217 = $2,170.

Total for those Part A hospital and SNF charges: $1,736 + $2,170 = $3,906.

Two things to note: his 5-day inpatient stay meets Medicare's 3-day minimum inpatient hospital stay requirement for SNF coverage (not counting the day he leaves the hospital), and Medicare covers SNF care only if his doctor certifies he needs daily skilled care. Also, doctors' services he gets in the hospital are covered under Part B, which generally pays 80% of the Medicare-approved amount — so he'd owe his share of those separately, and with Original Medicare there's no limit on what he pays out of pocket in a year unless he has other coverage.

answer.question: My mom turns 65 on March 12. When can she sign up for Medicare without paying a penalty, and when would her coverage start?
answer.answer:
Because her birthday (March 12) isn't on the first of the month, her Initial Enrollment Period is the 7 months that includes the 3 months before her birthday month, her birthday month, and the 3 months after — so December through June. Signing up during that window avoids a late enrollment penalty.

When coverage starts depends on when she signs up:
- If she signs up in the first 3 months of that period (December, January, or February), in most cases her coverage begins the first day of her birthday month — March 1.
- If she signs up in March (the month she turns 65) or in the last 3 months (April, May, or June), her coverage starts the first day of the month after she signs up.

She can sign up for Part A and/or Part B at SSA.gov/medicare/sign-up. Note that for Medicare drug coverage (Part D) there's also a late enrollment penalty if she goes 63 or more days in a row after her Initial Enrollment Period without Medicare drug coverage or other creditable prescription drug coverage.

answer.question: My husband is retiring in April and I'm 67 and covered by his employer's health plan. How long will I have to sign up for Part B, and does taking COBRA buy me more time?
answer.answer:
You have a Special Enrollment Period tied to your husband's job-based coverage. You can sign up for Part B any time while you're still covered by the group health plan, and then during the 8-month period that begins the month after the employment ends or the coverage ends, whichever happens first. Your coverage generally starts the first day of the month after you sign up; if you sign up while the job coverage is still in effect or within the first full month after it ends, you can ask to delay your Part B start date up to 3 months.

COBRA does not buy you more time. COBRA isn't considered coverage based on current employment, so the 8 months to sign up for Part B without a penalty runs from when the coverage based on current employment ends, whether or not you choose COBRA. And when the COBRA coverage itself ends, you generally aren't eligible for a Special Enrollment Period. The handbook also warns that if you have COBRA and you're eligible for Medicare, COBRA may only pay a small portion of your medical costs. If you sign up late outside a Special Enrollment Period, your monthly Part B premium may go up 10% for each full 12 months you could've had Part B but didn't sign up. answer.question: Mom has Original Medicare and nothing else. Is there a cap on what she can be charged out of pocket in a year, and would a Medicare Advantage plan cap it?
answer.answer:
No — with Original Medicare alone there's no yearly cap. The handbook says "There's no yearly limit on what you pay out of pocket, unless you have supplemental coverage—like Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap), Medicaid, employer, retiree, or union coverage." For Part B-covered services she usually pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount (the amount Medicare sets for a covered service) after she meets her deductible.

A Medicare Advantage Plan (Part C) does cap it: "Plans have a yearly limit on what you pay for covered Medicare services (which may include different limits for in-network and out-of-network services). Once you reach your plan's limit, you'll pay nothing for covered services for the rest of the year." The limit amount varies by plan, and Medicare Advantage plans may require using the plan's network and getting referrals. Note that if she has Part D drug coverage, out-of-pocket costs for Part D drugs are capped at $2,100 in 2026.

answer.question: My mother found a Medicare Advantage plan with a $0 monthly premium. Does that mean she would pay nothing each month for her Medicare?
answer.answer: No. A $0 monthly premium means the plan itself doesn't charge a premium — but she generally still pays the monthly Part B (Medical Insurance) premium, and the Part A premium too if she doesn't have premium-free Part A. Some Medicare Advantage Plans do help pay all or part of the Part B premium (sometimes called a "Medicare Part B premium reduction"), so it's worth checking whether this plan does. Also keep in mind that if the plan includes drug coverage, the plan's premium may include an amount for that coverage, and with a higher income she could owe an extra amount for Part D (in 2026, if income is above $109,000 filing individually or $218,000 married filing jointly). Besides premiums, she'd still have other out-of-pocket costs like copayments and deductibles when she uses services.

answer.answer: Yes. If your father has Medicare drug coverage (Part D), his yearly out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered by his plan are capped at $2,100 in 2026. Once he reaches that cap, he won't pay a copayment or coinsurance for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the calendar year. The cap counts his own out-of-pocket spending plus certain payments made by other people or entities, including Medicare's Extra Help program. Note this cap applies to Part D drugs — for drugs covered under Part B (ones a provider gives in a doctor's office or outpatient hospital setting), he generally pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount and the Part B deductible applies. His actual drug costs will also depend on things like whether his prescriptions are on his plan's list of covered drugs (formulary), what "tier" each drug is in, which pharmacy he uses, and whether he gets Extra Help.

The penalty is generally added to his monthly premium and he'd pay it for as long as he has Medicare drug coverage. He wouldn't pay the penalty if he gets Extra Help. The excerpts given don't include the formula used to calculate the penalty amount — that's on pages 83–85 of the handbook. answer.question: Dad is comparing Medigap Plan K and Plan L. What is the most each one would let him pay out of pocket in 2026, and how much of his costs do they cover?
answer.answer: In 2026, Plan K has an out-of-pocket yearly limit of $8,000 and Plan L has a limit of $4,000. Until he reaches that limit, Plan K pays 50% and Plan L pays 75% of these benefits: the Part B coinsurance or copayment, the blood benefit (first 3 pints), the Part A hospice care coinsurance or copayment, skilled nursing facility care coinsurance, and the Part A deductible — he pays the rest. Both plans pay 100% of Medicare Part A coinsurance and hospital costs (up to an additional 365 days after Medicare benefits are used), and neither covers the Part B deductible, Part B excess charges, or foreign travel emergency care. Once he meets the out-of-pocket yearly limit and the yearly Part B deductible ($283 in 2026), the plan pays 100% of covered services for the rest of the calendar year.

answer.question: When is the best time for my dad to buy a Medigap policy, and what happens if he waits?
answer.answer:
The best time is during his Medigap Open Enrollment Period — a 6-month period that begins the first month he has Medicare Part B (Medical Insurance) and is 65 or older. (Some states have additional Open Enrollment Periods.) Medigap is Medicare Supplement Insurance sold by private companies to help pay costs Original Medicare doesn't cover; he generally must have Part A and Part B before he can buy it.

If he waits until after that period, he may not be able to buy a Medigap policy at all, or it may cost more. In certain situations he may still have "guaranteed issue rights" to buy a policy outside the Open Enrollment Period, and some states provide additional special rights. Also, if he delays signing up for Part B because he has group health coverage based on his (or his spouse's) current employment, his Medigap Open Enrollment Period won't start until he gets Part B.

To learn more about his rights, he can call his State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) (phone numbers on pages 114–117) or his State Insurance Department, or visit Medicare.gov/medigap-supplemental-insurance-plans.

answer.question: Mom's doctor wants to set up home health care after her hip surgery. What will Medicare charge her for it, and does she have to be bedridden to qualify?
answer.answer:
Cost: she pays nothing for covered home health services. The only cost is for Medicare-covered durable medical equipment (like a walker or hospital bed), where she pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount, and the Part B deductible applies.

She does not have to be bedridden. Medicare covers home health services as long as she needs part-time or intermittent skilled services and is "homebound," which means any of these: she has trouble leaving home without help (a cane, wheelchair, walker, crutches, special transportation, or another person) because of an illness or injury; leaving home isn't recommended because of her condition; or she's normally unable to leave home because it's a major effort.

Two other requirements: a doctor or other health care provider (like a nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant) must assess her face-to-face before certifying that she needs home health services and must order the care, and a Medicare-certified home health agency must provide it. Covered care includes part-time or intermittent skilled nursing care, physical therapy, speech-language pathology, continued occupational therapy, medical social services, home health aide services, durable medical equipment, and medical supplies for use at home — up to 8 hours a day of skilled nursing and aide services combined, to a maximum of 28 hours a week (or up to 35 hours in some limited situations).

answer.question: Mom's cancer is terminal and her doctor brought up hospice. Who has to sign off before Medicare will cover it, and what would she have to pay?
answer.answer:
Who has to certify: a hospice doctor and your mom's own doctor (if she has one) must certify that she's terminally ill, meaning a life expectancy of 6 months or less. Your mom also has to sign a statement choosing hospice care (comfort care, also called palliative care) instead of other Medicare-covered treatments meant to cure her terminal illness and related conditions.

What she'd pay: nothing for hospice care itself; a copayment of up to $5 per prescription for outpatient drugs for pain and symptom management; and 5% of the Medicare-approved amount for inpatient respite care (care in a Medicare-approved facility so a caregiver can rest, up to 5 days each time). Medicare won't pay room and board where she lives, unless the hospice medical team decides she needs short-term inpatient care to manage pain and other symptoms.

Note that Original Medicare is billed for hospice care even if she's in a Medicare Advantage Plan, and Medicare still pays covered benefits for health problems unrelated to the terminal illness. For more on hospice and to find Medicare-approved providers, contact her plan or visit Medicare.gov/care-compare.

answer.question: Mom has been badly depressed since Dad died and wants to see a therapist. Does Medicare cover that, and what will she pay?
answer.answer:
Yes. Medicare covers outpatient mental health care for conditions like depression, including counseling or psychotherapy — individually, in a group, with family, or in a crisis. Covered providers include a psychiatrist or other doctor, clinical psychologist, marriage and family therapists, mental health counselors, clinical nurse specialist, clinical social worker, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant, and the visits can be in a doctor's or other provider's office, a hospital outpatient department, or by telehealth.

Cost: with Original Medicare, for Part B-covered services you usually pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount (the amount Medicare sets for the service) after you meet your deductible. If your mom is in a Medicare Advantage Plan, out-of-pocket costs vary by plan, so she should check with her plan.

Separately, Medicare also covers one depression screening per year in a primary care setting, and she pays nothing for that screening if the doctor accepts assignment.

Portugal is outside the U.S., and "Original Medicare generally doesn't cover medical care outside the U.S." The handbook notes you may be able to buy a Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap) policy — private insurance that fills gaps in Original Medicare — that covers emergency care outside the U.S. To check on Medigap options with foreign travel emergency coverage, they can contact their State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) at shiphelp.org.

answer.question: Mom spent three nights in the hospital but the billing office says she was under observation the whole time, never admitted. She needs a skilled nursing facility now. Will Part A pay for it?
answer.answer:
Most likely not. Medicare covers short-term skilled nursing facility (SNF) care only after a 3-day minimum medically necessary **inpatient** hospital stay (not counting the day she leaves the hospital), for an illness or injury related to that stay. The handbook is explicit that you're an inpatient only when the hospital formally admits you with a doctor's order, and that you're an outpatient if you're getting observation services — "even if you spend the night in the hospital." So nights spent under observation don't count toward the 3 days.

Two things worth checking:
- There are exceptions. She may not need the 3-day inpatient stay if her doctor participates in an Accountable Care Organization (ACO) approved for a Skilled Nursing Facility 3-Day Rule Waiver — ask the provider. Medicare Advantage Plans may also waive the 3-day minimum; contact the plan.
- If she was under observation more than 24 hours, the hospital must give her a "Medicare Outpatient Observation Notice" (MOON) explaining why she's an outpatient and how it affects what she pays for care after she leaves. The handbook also says you now have appeal rights when a hospital changes your status from inpatient to outpatient if you meet certain conditions — see page 101 or Medicare.gov/providers-services/claims-appeals-complaints/appeals/original-medicare.

If she does qualify, in 2026 she pays $1,736 at the start of a benefit period, then $0 a day for days 1–20, $217 each day for days 21–100, and all costs from day 101 on.

answer.question: My father moved to the U.S. at 58 and has only about 6 years of work here. Does he have to pay for Part A, how much in 2026, and what happens if he puts it off?
answer.answer:
The handbook doesn't spell out how many years of work are needed, so I can't confirm from these excerpts whether your father qualifies for premium-free Part A. What it says is: you usually pay no monthly Part A premium if you or your spouse paid Medicare taxes while working for a certain amount of time ("premium-free Part A"). If he isn't eligible for premium-free Part A, he may be able to buy it, and in 2026 the premium is either $311 or $565 each month, depending on how long he or his spouse worked and paid Medicare taxes.

If he isn't eligible for premium-free Part A and doesn't buy it when first eligible, his monthly premium may go up 10%, and he'd pay the higher premium for twice the number of years he could have had Part A but didn't sign up (for example, 2 years without signing up means a 10% higher premium for 4 years). Note that in most cases, if he chooses to buy Part A he must also have Part B and pay monthly premiums for both; if he chooses not to buy Part A, he can still buy Part B if eligible. The standard Part B premium in 2026 is $202.90.

For help paying the Part A premium, the handbook points to pages 91–92, and for questions about paying for Part A, visit Medicare.gov or call 1-800-MEDICARE. To check his specific work-credit eligibility, contact Social Security.

answer.question: Mom's only income is her Social Security check and she's struggling to pay her Medicare premiums. Is there a program that would help, and would it do anything for her drug costs?
answer.answer:
Yes — there are two programs, and they work together.

**Medicare Savings Programs** are state programs that help pay Medicare costs, including Part B premiums and other Medicare costs. If you don't think you qualify, you should still apply — contact your State Medical Assistance (Medicaid) office to get started. For your state's Medicaid office number, visit Medicaid.gov/about-us/where-can-people-get-help-medicaid-chip or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227); TTY users can call 1-877-486-2048.

**Extra Help** is the program for drug costs. If she has limited income and resources, it helps pay some Medicare drug costs, like premiums, deductibles, and coinsurance, and if she joins a Medicare drug plan or a Medicare Advantage Plan with drug coverage she won't pay a Part D late enrollment penalty. She may qualify if her yearly income and resources are below these 2025 limits: single person — less than $23,475 income and less than $17,600 in resources; married person living with a spouse and no other dependents — less than $31,725 and less than $35,130. In some situations she may qualify even with a higher income.

She qualifies automatically for Extra Help if she has full Medicaid coverage, gets help from her state Medicaid program to pay her Part B premiums and other Medicare costs, or gets Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits — Medicare mails a purple letter in that case, and she doesn't need to apply.

If she didn't qualify automatically, she can apply any time at SSA.gov/extrahelp. Applying for Extra Help also begins the application process for a Medicare Savings Program — Social Security sends information to her state to start it, unless she tells them not to on the application. For help with questions about Extra Help, call her State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) (see pages 114–117 or shiphelp.org) or 1-800-MEDICARE, TTY 1-877-486-2048.

answer.question: Mom is in a Medicare Advantage plan and wants to move to a different one for next year. When can she make that change, and when would the new plan kick in?
answer.answer:
She has two main chances:

1. **Open Enrollment Period (ends December 7)** — if she switches to a different Medicare Advantage Plan during this period, the new coverage starts January 1, as long as the plan gets her enrollment request by December 7.

2. **Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period, January 1 – March 31** — because she's already in a Medicare Advantage Plan, she can switch to another Medicare Advantage Plan (with or without drug coverage) during this period. She can only make one change during this period, and the new coverage starts the first of the month after the plan gets her request.

She might also be able to switch at other times if she qualifies for a Special Enrollment Period (for example, if she moves or loses other insurance coverage), or through the 5-star Special Enrollment Period (December 8 to November 30 the following year) if a plan with a 5-star quality rating is available in her area. Otherwise, she generally can't change plans during the year.

answer.question: Mom joined a Medicare Advantage plan in January and already regrets it. It's now February. Can she move to a different plan, and how many times can she change?
answer.answer: Yes. Because it's February, she's in the Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period, which runs January 1 to March 31. During this period, if she's in a Medicare Advantage Plan (with or without drug coverage) she can switch to another Medicare Advantage Plan, or drop her plan and return to Original Medicare (and also join a separate Medicare drug plan). But she can only switch plans once during this period — one change only — and the new coverage starts the first of the month after the plan gets her request. If she's returning to Original Medicare and joining a separate Medicare drug plan, she doesn't need to contact her Medicare Advantage Plan to disenroll; the disenrollment happens automatically when she joins the drug plan. One other note: if she just became eligible for Medicare and joined during her Initial Enrollment Period, she can switch to another Medicare Advantage Plan or go back to Original Medicare within the first 3 months she has Medicare. She may also have other chances if she qualifies for a Special Enrollment Period (for example, if she moves or loses other coverage), or through the 5-star Special Enrollment Period if a plan with a 5-star quality rating is available in her area.

answer.question: Mom is down to two Medicare Advantage plans, an HMO and a PPO. Would she have to pick a primary care doctor or get referrals, and what happens if she sees a doctor outside the network?
answer.answer:
The two plan types work differently:

HMO Plan — In most cases she would need to choose a primary care doctor, and in most cases she'd need a referral to see a specialist (some services, like yearly mammogram screenings, don't require a referral). She generally must get care from providers in the plan's network, except for emergency care, out-of-area urgent care, or temporary out-of-area dialysis. If she gets non-emergency care outside the network without authorization, she may have to pay the full cost. Some HMOs, called HMO Point-of-Service (HMOPOS) Plans, may let her get some out-of-network services for a higher copayment or coinsurance.

PPO Plan — She would not have to choose a primary care doctor, and in most cases no referral is needed for a specialist. A PPO has network providers, but she can also use out-of-network providers for covered services, usually for a higher cost, if the provider agrees to treat her and hasn't opted out of Medicare. Emergency and urgent care are always covered. Costs are usually lower with in-network ("preferred") providers.

For details about the specific plans she's considering, check with the plan or visit Medicare.gov.

answer.question: Dad's drug plan puts his medicine on an expensive tier and his doctor says the cheaper ones won't work for him. Can he ask the plan to charge him less, and how does that work?
answer.answer:
Yes. This is called asking the plan for an "exception." If your dad's drug is on a higher (more expensive) tier and his prescriber — his doctor or other provider who's legally allowed to write prescriptions — thinks he needs that drug instead of a similar drug on a lower tier, your dad or his prescriber can ask the plan for an exception to get a lower coinsurance or copayment for the higher tier drug. In other words, he can ask to pay less for a higher tier drug because he or his prescriber believe he can't take any of the lower tier drugs for the same condition.

The request goes to the plan, not the pharmacy: the plan's first decision about your dad's benefits is called a "coverage determination," and he has the right to get a written explanation of it. He'll get a coverage determination decision when he asks the plan to make an exception to its rules. For more information, the handbook points to Medicare.gov/providers-services/claims-appeals-; you can also contact the plan directly or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227); TTY users can call 1-877-486-2048.

answer.answer:
Here's what the 2026 Medigap chart shows for those two choices:

**Plan N** — It pays 100% of the Part B coinsurance, but you pay a copayment of up to $20 for some office visits and up to a $50 copayment for emergency room visits that don't result in an inpatient admission. Plan N also doesn't cover the Part B deductible ($283 in 2026) or Part B excess charges (the amount a doctor can charge above the Medicare-approved amount).

**High-deductible Plan G** — Plans F and G also offer a high-deductible version in some states. With it, you must pay Medicare-covered costs (coinsurance, copayments, and deductibles) up to the deductible amount of $2,950 in 2026 before your policy pays anything. Plan G doesn't cover the Part B deductible either, though it does cover Part B excess charges.

Note that Medigap premiums differ by plan and insurer, and the handbook doesn't list them here. Your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) can help compare specific policies — the phone numbers are on pages 114–117.

answer.question: Dad has had a Medigap policy for years but wants to try a Medicare Advantage plan. If he hates it, can he get his Medigap policy back?
answer.answer:
Maybe — but only under limited conditions, so he should be careful before dropping the Medigap policy.

If he drops a Medigap policy to join a Medicare Advantage Plan for the first time, he gets a single 12-month period (called his "trial right period") to get his Medigap policy back if the same insurance company still sells it once he returns to Original Medicare. If that policy isn't available, he can buy certain Medigap policies, depending on state law and whether he's new to Medicare on or after January 1. Outside that trial right period, the handbook warns he may not be able to get the same policy back — or in some cases any Medigap policy — and he might have to pay more, depending on his state's Medigap enrollment rules and his situation.

Two other points: Medigap policies mostly don't cancel automatically when he joins a Medicare Advantage Plan, so he must contact his insurance company if he wants to cancel, and he can't use Medigap to pay Medicare Advantage copayments, deductibles, or premiums. Generally he can return to Original Medicare if he's within the first 12 months of joining the Medicare Advantage Plan, or during the Open Enrollment or Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period, or with a Special Enrollment Period.

For details on his state's rules, he can call his State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) or his State Insurance Department, or visit Medicare.gov/health-drug-plans/medigap/ready-to-buy/change-policies.

answer.question: How much would a Medigap Plan G policy cost my dad per month?
answer.answer: The handbook doesn't list a price for Plan G — Medigap premiums are set by the private insurance companies that sell the policies, so there's no single monthly amount. It explains that with Medigap "you pay a monthly premium to a private insurance company in addition to the monthly Part B premium you pay to Medicare," and that "The costs can vary between plans offered by different companies for exactly the same coverage, and may go up as you get older." Some states limit Medigap premium costs, and if he's under 65 and able to buy a policy at all, it may cost more. To find actual prices for your dad's area, use Medicare.gov/medigap-supplemental-insurance-plans, or call his State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) (phone numbers are on pages 114–117) or his State Insurance Department.
